59453-a-short-list-of-scientific-books-p:
The short title list of E and F N Spon, dated September 1915, catalogues the firm's scientific books from 57 Haymarket, London. The firm, established in 1830, was sole English agent for Myron C Clark, Spon and Chamberlain, and the Business Code Company of New York. A contents page sorts the stock by trade: agriculture, architecture, artillery, aviation, bridges, cement, civil engineering, and dozens more. Each entry gives the author, the illustration count, the page count, the size, and the net price in shillings.

Agriculture opens with Boyce on hemp at 2s 6d net and French on farm drainage at 4s 6d net. Building titles include Allsop on the Turkish bath and Bales on the builder's clerk. The list is itself the work here, a priced catalogue of some fifty pages. It shows what a technical bookseller stocked on the eve of the motor age.
64591-publications-of-william-rider-son-:
Publications of William Rider and Son is a London publisher's catalogue, listing the firm's books with their prices. The catalogue leads with the New Thought Library, a series in crimson cloth with gilt tops. The series, the catalogue says, was designed to include only the best works in this class of literature. Sixteen volumes were ready when the list was printed.

The titles show what New Thought meant to its readers. Charles Godfrey Leland's book on strong will teaches self hypnotism for developing memory and mind power. Four volumes gather the essays of Prentice Mulford, including The Gift of the Spirit and The Gift of Understanding. Oliver Huckel offers Mental Medicine from a spiritual standpoint. Doctor Paul Dubois of Berne writes on the education of self and self control. Most volumes cost three shillings and sixpence.
71749-history-of-the-united-co-operative:
William Reid wrote the history of the United Co-operative Baking Society, printed in Glasgow in 1920. The book is a fifty years record, from 1869 to 1919, of a society that baked bread for co-operative stores in Scotland. Its central premises in Glasgow stand in the front plate.

Reid calls his work a plain, unvarnished tale of difficulties met and overcome. He wished he had time to dwell on the old enthusiasts who laid the base of the society and the hard world they faced. In a hurry, he still gives their faith, which refused to be dismayed, and the triumph that could be seen in the works. The book is a record for members and a slice of Scots working life.
75562-the-assassination-bureau-ltd:
The Assassination Bureau is a novel begun by Jack London. Robert Fish completed it from London's own notes after his death. McGraw-Hill first published the finished book in 1963. The story opens with a visitor shown into a strange apartment.

The caller is handsome, dark-eyed, and clearly ill at ease. A deaf-mute servant has just shown him in and left the room. The visitor can scarcely keep himself from shivering as he waits. Nothing in the room explains his fear at first sight. A friend's account of an earlier visit has warned him what to expect. The bureau of the title is a firm that deals in murder for hire. Its affairs are run with the cold order of a business office. London left the tale unfinished, and Fish built its ending from the author's papers.
